title: Salazar Says Trump Was 'Receptive' After She Warned Hispanic Voters Feel Betrayed
excerpt: The Florida Republican, in a rare GOP break with the president, told CBS she had a "very good conversation" with Trump after her campaign ad said his immigration enforcement had "gone too far."
body:
• Rep. María Elvira Salazar said President Trump was "very receptive" when she warned him by phone that Hispanic voters feel "betrayed" by his immigration enforcement, in a CBS "Face the Nation" interview Sunday.
  • The call followed her Sept. 17 campaign ad — a rare on-camera break with Trump by a GOP incumbent — in which she said enforcement had "gone too far" and cited ICE data that half of July's detainees had no criminal record.
  • Trump, who endorsed Salazar for reelection, said Friday he disagreed with her but understood her position; a White House official confirmed the phone call.
  • The episode lands amid sinking poll numbers: Gallup has 62% of Americans disapproving of Trump's handling of immigration, and Hispanic approval has fallen to 25% from 44% before he took office.

Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a three-term Republican congresswoman from a heavily Hispanic Miami district, said Sunday that President Donald Trump was "very receptive" when she warned him directly that his immigration enforcement push is alienating the Hispanic voters who helped return him to the White House — capping a week in which one of his own party's incumbents broke publicly with the signature policy of his second term.

"He was a gentleman, very courteous, very receptive," Salazar told CBS News' "Face the Nation" on Sunday, describing a phone call with the president after she released a 30-second campaign ad Thursday addressing him on camera. "Sir, you have this moment in history where you can keep the pot of gold that you brought to the GOP in 2024," she said she told him. "No other president was able to convince the Hispanics to vote 55 points for a GOP president. Please preserve that fortune that you have brought to the party."

A remarkable on-camera break

Salazar's ad, released Sept. 17, was extraordinary by the standards of a party that rarely criticizes Trump in public. Standing before the White House, she told the camera: "Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far." The ad cited Immigration and Customs Enforcement data to claim that half of the roughly 50,000 people detained in July had no criminal convictions or pending charges, and warned: "Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policies. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."

"17 campaign ad — a rare on-camera break with Trump by a GOP incumbent — in which she said enforcement had "gone too far" and cited ICE data that half of July's detainees had no criminal record."

She closed the ad with an appeal to history, urging Trump to "be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism" — and insisted she was not asking for amnesty but for immigrants to be given "a dignified life in this promised land."

Trump, who gave Salazar his "Complete and Total Endorsement" for reelection in the 2026 midterms earlier this year, responded Friday in the Oval Office. He said he had seen the ad and disagreed with it — "I disagree with her," he told reporters — while adding that he understood her position. "She's a nice person," he said. "I got her elected. Without me she wouldn't have gotten elected." A White House official confirmed to CNN that the two spoke by phone, without elaborating on the conversation.

Polls show the political risk

Salazar's warning is rooted in numbers her party is watching closely. A Gallup survey found 62% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of immigration. An Associated Press-NORC poll in October put Hispanic approval of Trump at just 25%, down from 44% shortly before he took office in 2025. A Fox News poll found his immigration approval at 43%, with 53% of voters saying ICE enforcement has gone too far.

The stakes are concrete in Salazar's backyard. Her district in Miami-Dade County is about three-quarters Hispanic, and Trump carried it by nearly 15 points in 2024, becoming the first Republican presidential candidate in more than three decades to win the county. A Hart Research/TelevisaUnivision survey this month found Hispanic voters in Florida battleground House districts favoring Democrats by 13 points, with more than 60% holding unfavorable views of Trump's performance.

The backlash has been building for months. Trump's deportation push has roiled communities, sparked protests against ICE, and triggered a battle in Congress over agency reforms. The issue intensified after the shooting deaths of two U.S. citizens, Alex Pretti and Renee Good, during an immigration enforcement operation in Minneapolis — after which Trump recalibrated his approach amid public outcry.

The diaspora angle

Salazar's core argument — "the average American understands the difference between the narco and the nanny and the gangster and the gardener" — resonates beyond Hispanic communities. For the Indian diaspora, immigration enforcement is not an abstract debate: H-1B workers recently lost the 60-day grace period after layoffs, social-media vetting has expanded to more visa categories, and mixed-status families live with the daily arithmetic of enforcement. A recalibration that distinguishes criminal threats from working families is exactly what legal-immigration advocates, including Indian American groups, have been asking for.

What to watch

Whether Trump's "receptive" tone translates into policy remains the open question. Salazar argued the president "gets it" because of his background in construction and hospitality — industries that employ large immigrant workforces — and blamed his advisers, saying "some of his advisers are compromising his legacy." With the midterms weeks away and Hispanic support slipping, the administration faces a choice between the deportation-maximalism that defined its first months and the course correction Salazar is urging. Her bet: that Trump, the only Republican to crack the Hispanic vote at this scale, will not want to be the one who gives it back.
